children.innerHTML: Jonas Riis · designer by day, maker by year
Every January I pick one project with my hands in mind and my calendar against me. It ships by December 31 or it doesn't count. Six years in, six things exist.
fig. 0: the tools that made them
A small-batch hand balm for cyclists, from beeswax to labels. Recipe seven finally survives a rainy century ride.
A 40 m² allotment taken from moss to first harvest. Fourteen crops, three failures, one extremely confident fox.
Rebuilt a 1962 log cabin with my dad. New roof, old bones, zero right angles, one properly stubborn stove.
Brazed a steel road frame in a rented corner of a friend's workshop. Eleven months of filing, one perfect first ride.
One three-legged stool a month until one stopped wobbling. Number nine did. Numbers one through eight are firewood.
Three hundred thrown pots, twelve survivors. The kitchen still uses all twelve, which feels like a verdict.
Why one a year? Because the year I tried twelve side projects, zero shipped. A year is long enough to learn a craft's first honest lesson and short enough that quitting feels louder than finishing.
Know a craft I should lose a year to? Make your case.

meta_description: Jonas Riis makes one personal project a year: a balm, a garden, a cabin, a bike frame, a stool, 300 pots.
